power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: A hallmark of the mature human memory system is the ability to extract commonalities across experiences while preserving details that distinguish individual events.
Although research 20 suggests that memory generalization emerges earlier than memory specificity, their developmental trajectories and interrelations remain poorly understood.
Here, we examined the development of generalization and multiple aspects of memory specificity in children aged 4 to 8 years, assessed at two timepoints one year apart (NTP1 = 170; NTP2 = 119).
We found that generalization improved more rapidly than memory specificity during early childhood.
25 Moreover, longitudinal changes in generalization and specificity were unrelated, suggesting distinct developmental trajectories.

These findings reveal an early developmental advantage for generalization over specificity, potentially reflecting an adaptive prioritization of extracting environmental regularities over retaining unique details of individual experiences.

Human memory must balance two competing demands: extracting regularities across experiences to facilitate generalization in similar but new situations versus preserving the details that keep individual experiences distinct (1, 2).
text.formatted: Human memory must balance two competing demands: extracting regularities across experiences to facilitate generalization in similar but new situations versus preserving the details that keep individual experiences distinct <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: These complementary capacities, generalization and specificity, respectively, are fundamental to adaptive cognition (3) (4) (5).
text.formatted: These complementary capacities, generalization and specificity, respectively, are fundamental to adaptive cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: But how do they emerge in typically developing children?
35 Prominent theoretical perspectives propose that specific memories constitute the foundation from which generalized knowledge emerges.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> Prominent theoretical perspectives propose that specific memories constitute the foundation from which generalized knowledge emerges.

text.text: Computational models suggest that generalizations arise through operations over specific episodic representations (6) or that they develop gradually from individual memories via consolidation (7, 8).
text.formatted: Computational models suggest that generalizations arise through operations over specific episodic representations <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref> or that they develop gradually from individual memories via consolidation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8)</ref>.

text.text: In line with these models, several theoretical frameworks addressing the ontogenetic development of human memory endorse a "generalization-from-specificity" account.
This view emphasizes that abstract knowledge structures are built upon initially discrete and instance-bound experiences (3, 9).
text.formatted: This view emphasizes that abstract knowledge structures are built upon initially discrete and instance-bound experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9)</ref>.

text.text: However, a growing body of developmental research challenges the generalization-fromspecificity account.

Evidence from studies on memory development indicates an early emergence 5 of generalized semantic knowledge derived from regularity extraction, such as word learning (10), category acquisition (11), and routine-event script knowledge (12).
text.formatted: Evidence from studies on memory development indicates an early emergence 5 of generalized semantic knowledge derived from regularity extraction, such as word learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref>, category acquisition <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref>, and routine-event script knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, this knowledge is more robust in infancy and early childhood than memory for specific details, including object-context associations (13) (14) (15) and detailed item representations (16, 17).
text.formatted: Moreover, this knowledge is more robust in infancy and early childhood than memory for specific details, including object-context associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(15)</ref> and detailed item representations (16, 17).

text.text: Contrary to adults (18, 19), recent findings suggest that generalization performance in children 10 depends less on detailed and context-specific episodic memory (20, 21).
text.formatted: Contrary to adults (18, 19), recent findings suggest that generalization performance in children 10 depends less on detailed and context-specific episodic memory <ref type="bibr">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: These results make a case for a "generalization-before-specificity" account.

At the intersection of functional and computational taxonomies of memory, an alternative, process-based framework proposes that memory development reflects a hippocampally mediated rebalancing between different representational modes (1, 2).
text.formatted: At the intersection of functional and computational taxonomies of memory, an alternative, process-based framework proposes that memory development reflects a hippocampally mediated rebalancing between different representational modes <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, early childhood is 15 initially characterized by a dominance of generalized representations, consistent with pattern categorization processes.
text.formatted: Specifically, early childhood is <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> initially characterized by a dominance of generalized representations, consistent with pattern categorization processes.

text.text: Subsequent development increasingly supports more specific and differentiated memory representations, associated with pattern separation and completion (1, 16).
text.formatted: Subsequent development increasingly supports more specific and differentiated memory representations, associated with pattern separation and completion <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr">16)</ref>.

text.text: These processes are thought to coexist across development, becoming more flexibly and adaptively deployed with age.

Empirical support for this framework has accumulated over recent 20 years (4, 5, 20), with studies investigating the behavioral readouts of component processes: pattern categorization via generalization (22) (23) (24), pattern separation via mnemonic discrimination (5, 16, 25), and pattern completion via cued retrieval (26, 27).
text.formatted: Empirical support for this framework has accumulated over recent 20 years <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5,</ref> <ref type="bibr">20)</ref>, with studies investigating the behavioral readouts of component processes: pattern categorization via generalization <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(24)</ref>, pattern separation via mnemonic discrimination <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25)</ref>, and pattern completion via cued retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27)</ref>.

text.text: The available evidence suggests that at least pattern separation and completion follow partially independent developmental trajectories (28).
text.formatted: The available evidence suggests that at least pattern separation and completion follow partially independent developmental trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: Together, this process-based approach argues that age-related 25 improvements do not reflect a unitary increase in memory capacity.
text.formatted: Together, this process-based approach argues that age-related <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> improvements do not reflect a unitary increase in memory capacity.

text.text: Rather, they portray an increasing equilibration of the computations necessary for multiple mnemonic demands.
A key prediction of this generalization-before-specificity account has not yet been directly tested.
The existing literature so far relied near-exclusively on cross-sectional investigations (29).
text.formatted: The existing literature so far relied near-exclusively on cross-sectional investigations <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches are inherently limited in their ability to characterize developmental dynamics 30 within individuals (30, 31) and, crucially, cannot determine whether generalization and specificity differ in rates of change across development.
text.formatted: Such approaches are inherently limited in their ability to characterize developmental dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30</ref> within individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31)</ref> and, crucially, cannot determine whether generalization and specificity differ in rates of change across development.

text.text: As a result, this prediction of the generalization-before-specificity account, that generalization should develop earlier and more rapidly than specificity, remained largely untested.

Addressing this question requires longitudinal data that track multiple memory processes within the same children over time, an approach that 35 is methodologically demanding and, therefore, rare (29).
text.formatted: Addressing this question requires longitudinal data that track multiple memory processes within the same children over time, an approach that <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> is methodologically demanding and, therefore, rare <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(29)</ref>.

text.text: Using a cohort-sequential longitudinal design, we followed children over a one-year period spanning early to middle childhood.
Within a single task, we assessed generalization alongside multiple forms of memory specificity, including context binding as well as memory for conceptual and perceptual details (20, 21).
text.formatted: Within a single task, we assessed generalization alongside multiple forms of memory specificity, including context binding as well as memory for conceptual and perceptual details <ref type="bibr">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21)</ref>.

text.text: This approach enabled a direct comparison of how 40 generalization and different facets of memory specificity evolve over development.
text.formatted: This approach enabled a direct comparison of how <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">40</ref> generalization and different facets of memory specificity evolve over development.

text.text: Consistent with the generalization-before-specificity account (1), we show that generalization exhibits earlier and more rapid developmental gains, whereas improvements in memory specificity are more gradual and independent of one another.
This temporal dissociation provides the first longitudinal evidence that generalization and specificity differ in their developmental 45 timing.

These findings demonstrate that asynchrony of change in component processes is a hallmark of human memory development, offering an empirical foundation for a process-level account (7, 32, 33) of mnemonic maturation (1, 29).
text.formatted: These findings demonstrate that asynchrony of change in component processes is a hallmark of human memory development, offering an empirical foundation for a process-level account <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">33)</ref> of mnemonic maturation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">29)</ref>.

text.text: To characterize rates of change in memory generalization and specificity across early and middle 5 childhood, we collected two-timepoint longitudinal data spaced one year apart from children aged 4 to 8 years.

We used a cohort-sequential design in which all children were assessed at timepoint 1 (TP1), and all but the oldest cohort (8-year-olds at TP1) returned for reassessment one year later at timepoint 2 (TP2; see Fig. 1A for a schematic depiction of the cohort sequential design and an overview of inter-assessment intervals by age).
text.formatted: We used a cohort-sequential design in which all children were assessed at timepoint 1 (TP1), and all but the oldest cohort (8-year-olds at TP1) returned for reassessment one year later at timepoint 2 (TP2; see Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref> for a schematic depiction of the cohort sequential design and an overview of inter-assessment intervals by age).

text.text: On average, children came back 10 for reassessment 358 days after their first visit (SD = 20 days, Mdn = 354 days; also see table S1 for the time between assessments divided by age group).

text.text: The final sample included here comprised 170 children at TP1 and 120 children at TP2.

At each assessment, children completed the Collection Game Task (20, 21), which simultaneously assesses memory generalization and multiple aspects of memory specificity 15 within a unified paradigm (see Fig. 1B).

text.text: Children watched various characters appear in distinct contexts and collect items.
Each of the 20 characters appeared in four contexts and collected a unique item in each context.

Importantly, each character was consistently associated with a semantic category (e.g., kitchenware, musical instrument), which constrained the locations and items presented with that character. 20 Memory was subsequently probed across several within-participant task conditions.

text.text: In the generalization condition, children were asked to identify a novel same-category item that a given character would plausibly collect, indexing pattern categorization.
In the context binding condition, children were presented with a character-context pairing and were asked to identify the item collected in that specific context, thereby indexing pattern completion.

Finally, pattern 25 separation demands were assessed across two additional specificity conditions: (i) an itemconceptual condition, in which children selected the previously encountered item among two category-matched lures, and (ii) an item-perceptual condition, in which they identified the exact color variant of the item among perceptually similar alternatives.

Then, the item conceptual and item perceptual specificity conditions were always administered consecutively on the same item.
Specifically, the item conceptual specificity condition entailed children identifying the item that the character collected, presented among novel same-category lures.
After their response, children received corrective feedback before proceeding to the item perceptual specificity condition.
Here, children then identified the correct 5 exemplar seen at encoding, presented among perceptually variant lures.
If early childhood memory is organized to prioritize knowledge extraction, age-related gains should be steeper for generalization than for specificity in early childhood.

Together, these findings display a mixed pattern: generalization converges across tasks, whereas indices of specificity-particularly pattern completion and separation-appear weakly coupled, both within and across paradigms.
Generalization enables the formation of portable knowledge by allowing us to move beyond our direct experiences.
Especially early in development, learning environmental regularities may take precedence over preserving detailed representations of individual episodes.
Here, we tested whether memory generalization and multiple forms of memory specificity follow differential 5 within-person developmental trajectories across childhood.
We find that as children transition from preschool to school-aged years, generalization shows stronger and steeper longitudinal gains than memory specificity.

Thus, when children encounter experiences that contain both common structure and episode-specific information, their ability to derive generalities develops more rapidly than their ability to retrieve or retain specific details.

The present study provides the 10 first direct longitudinal evidence for a developmental generalization-before-specificity account (1), documenting an uneven maturation of component processes of memory.
These findings advance the theoretical understanding of memory development beyond prior work in two respects.

First, by showing that generalization and specificity differ in rates of developmental change, the data adjudicate between the generalization-before-specificity and 15 generalization-from-specificity accounts in a way that cross-sectional age comparisons cannot.

Second, the dissociable trajectories of generalization and different aspects of memory specificity extend the process-based framework (1) from a largely descriptive taxonomy of memory operations into a set of testable predictions about the relative timing of their developments.
This temporal dissociation also provides a process-level perspective on broader developmental 20 changes in memory.
Childhood is characterized by substantial gains in both episodic and semantic memory (42) (43) (44).

text.text: Generalization hinges upon on the detection and extraction of commonalities across related experiences and may thereby contribute to the 25 early growth of semantic memory, which is similarly stripped from the original encoding context.

In contrast, pattern separation and pattern completion support the retention and retrieval of distinctive information about individual events and may contribute to the more protracted development of episodic memory.
Generalization and specificity should not be directly equated with semantic and episodic memory, respectively.

Nevertheless, the present findings suggest that 30 the earlier emergence of semantic knowledge may partly reflect the earlier developmental strengthening of processes that support regularity extraction.
On the other hand, the slower maturation of detailed episodic memory may reflect a later and more gradual development of processes supporting event specificity.

text.text: Different forms of generalization differentially draw on specific representations, and this reliance varies across development (62, 63), enabling increasingly efficient joint use of general and specific representations.

A path towards reconciliation is to clarify that 15 generalization-before-specificity describes the relative timing across development, whereas generalization-from-specificity characterizes the task-dependent use of specific information to support particular forms of inference that differs across development.
The present findings also speak to the question of whether generalization and specificity reflect independent processes or are coupled through shared representations.

Consistent with 20 neurocomputational models that ascribe pattern categorization, separation, and completion to partially non-overlapping hippocampal subfields (37, 64), we find that their longitudinal changes are largely unrelated.
This suggests that the key mnemonic computations develop simultaneously, but along separable trajectories across childhood.
At the same time, gains in generalization are selectively associated with gains in conceptual specificity and converge across 25 tasks.

The selective coupling indicates that some forms of generalization may draw on shared representational capacities, such as the ability to retain the semantic features of experiences, and may develop along similar trajectories, even if inter-individual performance levels are not correlated.
The fact that we did not find an association between individual differences in change for memory 30 of contextual and perceptual details has important theoretical implications.

text.text: Within the traditional functional taxonomy of memory, both abilities are considered defining features of episodic memory, reflecting the retrieval of an episode's spatiotemporal context along with their perceptual details (65).

text.text: Adding to prior cross-sectional studies that did not find behavioral associations across individuals (4, 16, 28), our longitudinal analyses show that these two abilities 35 follow dissociable developmental trajectories when tracked within individuals over time.
This aligns with computational models proposing that pattern completion and pattern separation are distinct neural computations and make complementary contribution to remembering specific episodes.
Accordingly, treating episodic memory as a single construct may obscure meaningful developmental differences among individual processes that support it.
A computational 40 perspective helps explain how a seemingly unitary function can emerge from multiple underlying computations that develop in parallel.

A plausible neurodevelopmental basis for this pattern lies in the continued maturation of hippocampal circuitry across childhood and adolescence (5, 23, 66), and the hippocampus' role in both general and specific memory from early ontogeny (56, 67).

text.text: Its subfields are thought to 45 make partially distinct contributions to pattern categorization, separation, and completion, and their developmental profiles are not uniform.

In particular, earlier maturation of CA1 relative to dentate gyrus and CA3 (38, 39) provides a potential mechanism for the earlier emergence of regularity extraction relative to highly differentiated episodic representations.

text.text: Computational work that places CA1 central to statistical learning and generalization (36, 37) is consistent with the early ability to detect regularities in infancy.
However, the present behavioral findings cannot 5 establish this mechanism directly.

Longitudinal studies combining component process measures with high-resolution hippocampal imaging are needed to test whether differential subfield maturation drives the asynchronous developmental trajectories observed here.
Future research should also directly test the practical implications of these findings for early education.

Given that young children are biased toward regularity extraction before they reliably 10 encode episode-specific details, instructional approaches emphasizing the shared structure across experiences should promote early learning.

For example, grouping related examples together or explicitly highlighting the commonalities in a set of experiences, may be particularly wellmatched to how young children's memory systems naturally operate, compared to approaches that rely heavily on remembering one-off details.
As memory specificity processes mature later 15 and more gradually, curricula may also need to scaffold detail-oriented learning more explicitly in early childhood than in middle childhood.

text.text: We encourage future work to examine this interplay in applied educational settings.
In conclusion, we find that central component processes of memory differ in their developmental timing across early and middle childhood.

Generalization develops earlier and more rapidly and 20 is coupled with changes in conceptual specificity, whereas memory specificity improves more gradually and its different measures do not follow a common trajectory.

These findings support a process-based account of mnemonic maturation in which development reflects not a unitary increase in memory capacity, but asynchronous changes in the computations required to extract regularities and preserve event-specific information (1).

Such differential developmental pacing 25 may be adaptive: prioritizing the formation of portable general knowledge templates about the environment guides adaptive behaviors based on limited experience early in life (51), while laterdeveloping specificity supports more flexible retention of contexts, exceptions, and individual events.

text.text: Cartoon images of 20 characters, 80 contexts, and 180 black-and-white, line-drawn objects were selected from the Google Images search engine.
Unpopular and androgynous 5 characters were used to reduce the probability of children having pre-existing semantic knowledge about the characters.
Twenty categories of semantically congruent objects and contexts were chosen based on their probable familiarity to young children (e.g., musical, cooking, and medical objects).
Each character was arbitrarily assigned to a category (e.g., the character named 'Luntik' was be assigned to the category music).
Each character was placed in 10 four different contexts to create four encoding trial images for that character.
All four contexts images paired with a given character were semantically congruent with the character's assigned category (e.g., Luntik was placed on four perceptually distinct performance stages).
The 180 objects were chosen such that there were nine distinct objects for every category (e.g., the musical instrument category consisted of a guitar, a piano, a drum, a trumpet, etc.).
Every line-15 drawn object was manually painted with three distinct colors using Photoshop, resulting in a total set of 720 object images (180 objects x 4 color versions).
An additional two characters, eight backgrounds, and 18 objects were selected from Google Images for use in the training phase and as an example trial.
These additional stimuli were semantically unrelated to those used for the study and test phases of the experiment.
Procedure.

The experiment comprised two testing sessions: an immediate session conducted in the late afternoon or early evening on Day 1 and a delayed session conducted on the morning of Day 2, however we only report results from the immediate session here.
The immediate session consisted of two encoding-test blocks using non-overlapping stimulus sets.
Each block included character familiarization, an encoding phase, and a test phase.
The test phase comprised four 25 tasks assessing generalization, context binding, item conceptual specificity, and item perceptual specificity.
The immediate session lasted approximately 45 minutes.
(1) Training and Task Screening.
Prior to the encoding phase of the first block, children received training that illustrated the encoding and test procedure using two characters and categories that were not used in the main task.

The experimenter introduced both characters, presented a total of 30 8 encoding trials (4 per character, shown in an interleaved order) and subsequently children performed the test phase in the same manner as in the real experiment, only that children received corrective feedback during the training in each task condition.
This was done to ensure that children understand the task.

Importantly, on the generalization trials, children were given instructions to select the new item that the character would most likely add to their collection and 35 were also reminded of the category of objects the respective character had collected in the encoding trials.
The two generalization trials were then used to assess children's understanding of a collection of items and that items of the same category belong together.
Children who selected the correct item in at least one of the two trials of the generalization task were considered to have understood the task.
We excluded participants that failed on this task 40 screening at both timepoints or at the first if they did not come back for a second timepoint (n = 0).
(2) Character Introduction.
Children were then told that they would be introduced to some other new friends.
They were presented with images of each character sequentially and in a fixed order.
On each trial, the experimenter verbally introduced the character by name (e.g., "This is Luntik").
There were 10 characters per block.
(3) Encoding.
At encoding, children were told that each friend was making a collection of their favorite things, and that each friend would visit different places to find items for their collection.
Children were instructed to pay attention to the kinds of things that each friend liked.

In each 5 block, the encoding phase consisted of 40 trials, each comprising an image of a character in a context presented on the left side of the screen and an object presented on the right side of the screen (5 s, 0.5 s ITI).
Every character appeared in four encoding trials, each time in a different context and paired with a different object.
Critically, the context and objects paired with a given character were semantically related.

For instance, Luntik -a character assigned to the "music" 10 category -was seen on perceptually different performance stages and collected categoryconsistence objects such as a drum, a guitar, a horn, and an accordion.
One randomized fixed order of the encoding trials was created for all participants, with the only restriction being that the same character did not appear on consecutive trials.
(4) Test.
In the immediate session, the self-paced 3AFC test phase immediately followed the 15 encoding phase of each block.
There were four task conditions, administered in a fixed order across participants: (a) generalization, (b) context binding, (c) item conceptual specificity, (d) item perceptual specificity.
There were 10 test trials per task condition in each block.
Each task condition had 20 trials administered in a fixed randomized order across participants.
(a) Generalization.
Every test trial showed a character at the top of the screen and three objects 20 at the bottom of the screen.
Children were asked to choose one object that this friend would add to their collection.
All three objects were novel items that had not appeared in the encoding phase.
One object was the target -the correct item that belonged to the category assigned to that character.
The other two objects were lures -objects that belonged to different semantic categories assigned to two other characters.
Target selection indicates that participants 25 successfully made a novel inference based on the related episodes associated with a given character.
(b) Context Binding.
Every test trial showed an image of a character in one of that character's four encoding contexts at the top of the screen and three objects at the bottom.
Children were asked to choose the object previously found by the friend in that exact context.
All three objects 30 were seen with the character at encoding, but only one (i.e., target) was the item that appeared in that context.
The other two objects were lures -objects that would have been seen with the character, but that were paired with that character in different contexts.
Correct target selection would indicate that participants remembered the specific object-context co-occurrence.
Both subtasks were 35 linked, such that the item perceptual specificity trial immediately followed the item conceptual specificity trial for each character.
Every item conceptual specificity test trial started with a character at the top of the screen and three line-drawn objects at the bottom of the screen.
Children were asked which of the three objects the character had found for their collection.
All three objects belonged to the same category assigned to the character (e.g., musical instruments 40 for the trial of Luntik).
One object was the target -the correct item that had appeared at encoding.
The other two objects were lures -objects that belonged to the semantic category assigned to the character but had never appeared at encoding.
In the presence of conceptually similar lures, target selection indicated that participants remembered the objects' identities with high specificity.
Critically, all three objects were presented as color-stripped line-drawn versions, 45 because participants' memories for the perceptual details of the objects were tested subsequently.
After target selection, a red square appeared around the choice, and the experimenter provided feedback on whether children had selected correctly.

The item perceptual specificity trial then immediately followed, in which the same character was shown at the top of the screen with three objects below: one perceptually identical to the encoded object (target), and two perceptually 5 similar exemplars differing in color only.
Correct responses indicated memory for detailed perceptual attributes.

text.text: A fixed set of 15 ABC triads was created, each triad consisting of two animals (designated A and C) and one 15 scene (B).
From these triads, 30 unique animal-scene pairs (AB and BC) were constructed.
Procedure.
The task consisted of three encoding-direct associative memory test cycles.
After the three cycles, participants completed an associative inference test, followed by a procedural understanding check.
A single randomized order of study and test items was administered across all participants.
Total task duration was approximately 30 minutes.
20 (1) Encoding.
Children were told they would meet groups of animal friends, each planning a vacation, and would see each animal paired with its vacation destination.
The experimenter emphasized attentive viewing of each animal's selected destination.
Before the first encoding block, children completed two familiarization trials using an animal and a scene not included in the test set.

Each encoding block comprised 30 animal-scene (AB and BC) pairs, with each trial 25 presenting the scene on the right and the animal on the left side of the screen (3 s per trial, 0.5 s inter-trial interval).

Randomized orderings of AB and BC pairs were generated for each encoding block, with the constraints that (i) AB and BC pairs from the same triad did not appear consecutively, and (ii) each triad's AB pair preceded its BC pair.
Children were not informed of the relationship between AB and BC pairs, nor that inference questions would follow, at any 30 point prior to the associative inference test.
(2) Test.
Two test phases were administered: an associative memory test and an associative inference test.
(a) Associative Memory Test.
Immediately after each encoding block, children completed a selfpaced three-alternative forced choice (3AFC) memory test on the 30 directly learned (AB and 35 BC) pairs.
Trial order was fixed across participants.

Before the associative memory test began, the experimenter told the participant that they would now always see one of the animal friends on the top of the screen and that they should pick the place that this friend wanted to go on their next vacation from the three options on the bottom of the screen.
On each trial, an animal cue appeared at the top of the screen with three scene options below.
The target was the correct 40 paired scene, while the other two were scene lures from other triads.
Responses were indicated by pointing, and the experimenter entered answers via key press ('1', '2', or '3', corresponding to left, middle, or right).
No corrective feedback was provided.
(b) Associative Inference Test.

Upon completion of the three encode-test cycles, children were tested on their ability to infer the relationship between indirectly linked animal pairs (A and C), which had both been paired with the same scene (B).
Each triad contributed one test item, yielding 15 inference trials.
On each trial, animal C of a triad appeared as the cue at the top of the screen, with three animal options (all A animals from different triads) at the bottom.
Children 5 were instructed to choose the animal that wanted to visit the same place as the cue animal.
The target was the A animal from the same triad; the other two were lures.
No corrective feedback was provided.
(3) Procedural Understanding Screening.
To ensure comprehension of the task, a procedural understanding check followed the associative inference phase.
Children were told that there were 10 a few more friends who were late.
They were then shown three trials with a novel AB and BC pair from one triad as well as one single AB pair of a different triad.
After that, all were presented simultaneously on the screen and children were asked to select which of two animals (one target, one lure) would choose the same vacation place as the cue animal.
Correct responses on these trials indicated that children have understood the task instruction that animals who went 15 the same place would go on vacation together, without the memory demand.

We additionally excluded participants that failed on this procedural understanding screening at both timepoints or at the first if they did not come back for a second timepoint (n = 3: one four-year-old, one fiveyear-old, and one six-year-old).

text.text: To test whether children showed retest effects at TP2, we performed two-sample ttests for each subtask and each age range separately.

To do this, we compared the accuracy between children of the same age that came in for their first time (e.g. 5-year-olds at TP1) to those who came in for the second time but were the same age (e.g. 5-year-olds at TP2, i.e. 4-40 year-olds at TP1).
We corrected for multiple comparisons in each subtask by the number of tests, in the current case 4, using the Bonferroni-Holm method (73).
To test whether within-child changes in same construct were coupled between tasks, we examined change-change associations by calculating the TP1 and TP2 accuracy differences in each task.
We calculated correlations for the entire sample, controlling for age.

The change-change correlations of interest were (i) between the different task conditions within the collection game, (ii) between generalization performance in the Collection Game and associative inference performance in the Vacation Game -both were measures of generalization, and (iii) between context binding in Collection Game and direct associative 5 memory in Vacation Game -both were measures of pattern completion.
For the direct associative memory in Vacation Game, we used accuracy from the first test block, as this mirrors the one-shot learning in context binding from the Collection Game.

text.text: Here, we summarize the general design features relevant to the two timepoints analyzed in the current paper, along with the procedures for the Collection Game and Vacation Game Task.

The initial sample at the first measurement time point (TP1) included 180 children aged 4 (mean 10 age: 53.9 ± 3.25 months, n = 38; 19 females), 5 (mean age: 66.3 ± 3.18 months, n = 34; 14 females), 6 (mean age: 78.7 ± 3.92 months, n = 39; 17 females), 7 (mean age: 89.6 ± 3.51 months, n = 35; 18 females), and 8 (mean age: 102.3 ± 3.43 months, n = 34; 16 females).

Data from a total of 8 children were excluded from both timepoints: four children were retrospectively excluded due to a diagnosis of ADHD at a later time than their initial participation and four 15 children only completed the first of five experimental sessions at their initial measurement time point.
For the Collection Game, data from two additional children at TP 1 were missing due to experimenter error, resulting in 170 children from TP1 included.
For the Vacation Game, data from two additional children at TP 1 were missing due to early termination by the participant, resulting in 170 children from TP1 included.
